title: Spend by region and year

blocks.text: Three counties fund a shared fiber-backbone program, and each county's board approves its own yearly cap. The plan's model must report, for every county and every year, what the plan spends there, so a cap can be written against each number.

Write `spend_by_region_year(projects, x, years)` in `regional.py`. It returns a dict with one entry for every `(region, year)` pair (every region that has a project, every year in `years`), each a linear expression in the start variables `x[(pid, start_year)]`. A project's `cost_profile[k]` is what it spends in its k-th year of work, counting its start year as year 0. A cost that would fall in a year outside `years` belongs to no entry.
The tests fix a schedule and evaluate your expressions, so any correct expression passes. About eight lines in total.

In the lesson's notation, with $`R`$ the regions, $`P_r`$ the projects in region $`r`$, $`T_i`$ the start years of project $`i`$, $`c_{i,k}`$ its `cost_profile[k]` and $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ the start variables, you are writing the expression $`\text{spend}_{r,y}`$ for every $`r \in R`$ and $`y \in Y`$. Write it as a sum first (which pairs $`(i, t)`$ put money into year $`y`$?), then code it. A cap would then be the row $`\text{spend}_{r,y} \le \text{cap}_{r,y}`$.

cases.says: the spend of a one-region plan, summed over every year, is the cost of the projects it starts
a two-year project's start year carries only its first year's cost
a project spends in the very year it starts
a project whose second year costs more than its first spends that larger amount in its second year
a project's spend appears only in its own region's rows
a project started in the plan's last year spends in that year

origin.section: Build Spend as an Expression Once, and Every Budget Rule Reuses It

concepts: a project started in year t spends its k-th year's cost in year t + k
spend is built once as expressions and every money rule is a row on them
